## Abstract

It remains unclear whether lean non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) patients had worse outcomes. This study aims to investigate the long-term outcome of NAFLD in comparison to overweight and obese NAFLD using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) III. A total of 11860

participants (mean age, 43.4 years; 6498 [54.8%] women) were analyzed. NAFLD was assessed by hepatic ultrasonography and stratified into lean (body mass index, [BMI] < 25), overweight (BMI 25.0-29.9), and obese (BMI ≥ 30) subgroups. The Cox proportional hazards models were used to compute hazard ratios (HRs) and

95% CIs for the associations of NAFLD subgroups with risks of mortality. Lean NAFLD patients showed younger age and a lower prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance. During a median follow-up period of 276 months, 3484 (29.4%) all-cause mortality occurred. All NAFLD subgroups were associated with increased all-cause mortality risk compared with healthy controls. However, only lean NAFLD

was independently associated with all-cause mortality (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.03–1.47) after the adjustment of confounders. This national-wide cohort study showed that lean NAFLD was significantly associated with higher all-cause mortality. A more granular assessment was needed to further characterize the phenotypes of the lean

NAFLD population.

## Introduction

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) affects about 25% of the global population1. The widely recognized

risk factors for NAFLD include insulin resistance (IR) and obesity2. Therefore, the worldwide increase in NAFLD

prevalence was thought to be associated with the global epidemic of obesity3. However, NAFLD is increasingly

being recognized in non-obese individuals with a body mass index (BMI) < 25 kg/m2. These individuals are

labeled as lean NAFLD4,5.

Previous studies suggest that lean NAFLD is not a benign disease. Patients with lean NAFLD are not spared from nonalcoholic steatohepatitis and advanced fibrosis and are at risk of developing hepatic and extrahepatic

complications6,7. However, differences in long-term outcomes of lean NAFLD compared to overweight and obese NAFLD remain unclear. Studies investigating the outcomes of patients with lean NAFLD were scarce and presented disputable conclusions. It has been recognized that lean NAFLD patients in Asia had a better

prognosis compared with obese NAFLD patients8,9, while a recent study concluded that Caucasian lean

subjects with NAFLD share a similar long-term prognosis with non-lean counterparts10. There is also limited evidence that suggests that lean NAFLD had the highest risk of overall mortality compared with overweight or

obese11. The inconsistent conclusions might be a result of the diversity of study population, and most of the studies were limited by relatively small sample sizes or inadequate follow-up periods.

In this study, we aimed to describe baseline characteristics and explore the long-term outcomes of lean NAFLD

in comparison to overweight and obese NAFLD patients using national-wide US population-based data with a long duration of the follow-up period from the third National Health and Nutrition Survey (NHANES III) database.

## Methods

## Study design and population


<!-- Page 3 -->


Page 3/20

NHANES III was conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) from 1988 to 1994 in the United States. It aimed to evaluate the health and nutritional status of non-institutionalized US civilians through a nationally representative sample. The NHANES III study protocol received approval from the NCHS Institutional Review Board, and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. All analyses of this study were

in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE)

guidelines12.

Out of the 20,050 participants in NHANES III, 14,797 adults aged 20 to 74 underwent hepatic ultrasound examination. Those with ungradable (N = 127) or missing (N = 814) ultrasound results were excluded. Additionally, 1,261 participants were excluded due to viral hepatitis, and 465 were excluded due to excessive alcohol consumption. Nine participants lost to follow-up were also excluded. Furthermore, 261 participants with BMI < 18.5 kg/m2 or missing data were excluded due to the complex and less understood relationship between undernutrition and fatty liver. The final study cohort comprised 11,860 NHANES III participants (Fig. 1). Demographic, anthropometric, and laboratory measurements

Demographic characteristics, including age, sex, race/ethnicity, family poverty income ratio (FPIR), marital status, and health status, were collected by questionnaires. Race/ethnicity was categorized into four groups (Non-Hispanic White, Non-Hispanic Black, Mexican-American, and Other). FPIR was calculated as total family income divided by the poverty threshold, categorized into three groups (< 1.3, 1.3 to 3.5, ≥ 3.5). Marital status

was categorized into two groups (living with a partner, single), and health status was categorized into three groups (excellent or good, fair, poor). Body measurements, including height, weight, waist circumference, and

blood pressure, were obtained during physical examinations. BMI (kg/m2) was calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Blood tests included total cholesterol (TC) (mg/dL), triglyceride

(TG) (mg/dL), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) (mg/dL), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) (mg/dL), Lipoprotein(a) [LP(a)] (mg/dL), C-reactive protein (CRP) (mg/dL), fasting glucose (mg/dL), fasting insulin (uU/ml), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (IU/L), and γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT) (IU/L). IR was assessed using the homeostatic model assessment–insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) equation as follows: fasting

insulin (uU/mL) × fasting blood glucose (mmol/L) ÷ 22.513. We used a HOMA-IR score ≥ 2.5 as an indicator of IR. Diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertriglyceridemia were defined based on self-report or objective measurements. Smoking status and average alcohol consumption were self-reported. Smoking status was self-reported. The average alcohol consumption per day was calculated using the frequency and amount of alcohol consumed per drinking day. Definition of NAFLD and advanced fibrosis

The method for diagnosing fatty liver via gallbladder/hepatic ultrasound has been previously described14. Briefly, the hepatic ultrasonography was conducted using a Toshiba SSA-90A ultrasound machine (Tustin, CA) in

NHANES III adult participants (aged 20–74 years). The archived gallbladder ultrasound examination videotapes were reviewed by 3 board-certified radiologists between 2009 and 2010 to grade the presence of fat within the

hepatic parenchyma. The ultrasonographic findings were reported as normal versus mild, moderate, or severe hepatic steatosis. The intra-rater and inter-rater reliability (percent agreement) of these assessments were

91.3% and 88.7%, respectively15. In this study, NAFLD was defined as moderate or severe hepatic steatosis in

the absence of excessive alcohol consumption and other causes of chronic liver disease. Advanced fibrosis was determined based on non-invasive liver fibrosis scores. Patients with at least 1 of the 3 non-invasive liver

fibrosis scores indicated a high probability of advanced fibrosis (NAFLD fibrosis score > 0.676, fibrosis-4 > 2.67,

and aspartate aminotransferase to platelet ratio index > 1.5) were deemed to have advanced liver fibrosis16. Mortality ascertainment

Mortality data were obtained from the NHANES Public-Use Linked Mortality File linked to the National Death Index. The underlying cause of death 113 (UCOD_113) code was encoded by the definition of the International

Classification of Diseases, 9th Edition (ICD-9) for deaths through 1998, and ICD-10 for deaths from 1999 to

2015. Cause-specific mortalities were assessed including cardiovascular disease (CVD) (UCOD_113 code: 55–

64, 70) and cancer (UCOD_113 code: 19–43)16. The duration of follow-up was defined as the interval in months from the interview date to the date of death or through December 31, 2015, for participants without event. Statistical analysis

Participants with NAFLD were categorized into 3 subgroups based on BMI: (i) Lean NAFLD (BMI < 25 kg/m2), (ii)

Overweight NAFLD (25 ≤ BMI < 30 kg/m2), (iii) Obese NAFLD (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2)10,17. The means (standard deviation)/median [interquartile range] for normally/skewed distributed continuous variables and counts (percentage) of categorical variables were presented among comparison groups. Baseline characteristics were

compared using the t-test/standard non-parametric tests for normally/skewed distributed continuous variables

and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Multinomial Logistic Regression Analysis was applied to assess the associations between risk factors and the presence of NAFLD in 3 subgroups. The results were

presented as a forest plot. We used Cox proportional hazards models to determine hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations between NAFLD subgroups and risk of all-cause and cause-

specific mortality after adjustment for potential demographic and clinical confounders. The proportional hazards assumption was examined by creating time-dependent covariates in the models. No apparent violation

of the proportional hazards assumption was identified (p > 0.05). Survival was also evaluated using the

adjusted Kaplan–Meier curves. Statistical tests were 2-sided, and statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software, version 4.0.1 (R Core Team, Vienna, Austria). Ethics statement

NHANES is conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). The NCHS Research Ethics Review Committee reviewed and approved the NHANES

study protocol. All participants signed written informed consent.

## Results

## Baseline Characteristics

The prevalence of NAFLD in the study population was 22.6% (2675 of 11860). The baseline characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1. Older age, male, and Mexican-American race/ethnicity were

associated with the presence of NAFLD. Prevalence of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and hypercholesterolemia was higher in NAFLD patients than in those without NAFLD, while smoking was less

common (Table 1). Among 2675 NAFLD patients, 443 (16.6%) were classified as lean NAFLD, 940 (35.1%) were

identified as overweight NAFLD, and 1292 (48.3%) were categorized as obese NAFLD. Compared with overweight and obese NAFLD, lean NAFLD participants were younger, had a lower prevalence of metabolic


<!-- Page 5 -->


Page 5/20

comorbidities and better glycolipid metabolism profiles, with lower fasting glucose, HOMA-IR, TC, TG, and LDL-C levels and higher HDL-C levels. Of note, the Lp(a) level was highest in the lean NAFLD group, and CRP was

significantly higher in the obese NAFLD group. The liver enzyme test results (ALT and GGT) were poorer in

obese NAFLD than in lean NAFLD. The prevalence of advanced fibrosis was highest in obese group (Table 2).

In the lean NAFLD group, age (per 10 years increase odds ratio [OR]: 1.08, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.00- 1.16), Mexican-American race/ethnicity (OR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.18–1.91), diabetes (OR, 1.74; 95% CI, 1.21–2.50),

and smoking (OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.05–1.63) were independently associated with the presence of NAFLD while CRP (OR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.65-1.00) was negatively associated with the incidence of NAFLD (Fig. 2). Of note, several metabolic risk factors, including hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, and insulin resistance, though strongly associated with the presence of NAFLD in overweight and obesity groups, were not significant in the

association with NAFLD in the lean group (Fig. 2).

## Survival analysis

During a median follow-up period of 276 months (up to 326 months), 3484 (29.4%) all-cause deaths occurred. Among them, 2448 (20.6%) occurred in the individuals without NAFLD, 149 (1.3%), 383 (3.2%), and 504 (4.2%) occurred in lean, overweight, and lean NAFLD patients, separately. 741 deaths were CVD-related, and 823 deaths were cancer-related. The rates of all-cause mortality were 16.5, 20.7, and 19.5 per 1000 person-years for

lean, overweight, and obese NAFLD separately, with 3.0 excess deaths per 1000 person-years in obese NAFLD compared to lean NAFLD (Table 3). The univariable Cox model showed that compared to individuals without NAFLD, lean NAFLD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.34; 95% CI, 1.14–1.58), overweight NAFLD (HR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.53–

1.89), and obese NAFLD (HR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.45–1.76) were all associated with higher all-cause mortality risk. Multivariable model 1 adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, FPIR, health status, and smoking. Among three subgroups of NAFLD, both lean NAFLD (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.01–1.40) and obese groups (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.07–

1.30) were associated with higher all-cause mortality risk. In multivariable model 2, we further adjusted for waist circumference, hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, diabetes, insulin resistance, and advanced fibrosis, and only lean NAFLD was still associated with higher all-cause mortality risk (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.03–1.47) (Table 3). The adjusted Kaplan–Meier curves for all-cause mortality are shown in Fig. 3. When the analysis was

restricted to cause-specific mortality, individuals with overweight and obese NAFLD had 91% (HR 1.91; 95% CI 1.52–2.38) and 69% (HR 1.69; 95% CI 1.38–2.08) higher cardiovascular mortality risk than those without NAFLD, separately. However, this association attenuated and became insignificant after adjusting for potential

confounders. A similar pattern was also observed in the analysis of cancer mortality. There was no significant association between NAFLD subgroups and cardiovascular and cancer mortality.

## Discussion

We herein report details on the long-term outcome of lean NAFLD in comparison to overweight and obese

NAFLD patients. We noted a significant association between lean NAFLD and all-cause mortality independently of demographic characteristics and known metabolic risk factors in this longitudinal, nationally representative, US population-based study. In addition, our study added notable information to the field of lean NAFLD: (1)

smoking was independently associated with the presence of NAFLD only in the lean patients; (2) lean NAFLD patients presented better metabolic profiles in general, and traditional metabolic risk factors, especially insulin resistance, were not associated with the incidence of NAFLD in lean patients.

As research on lean NAFLD grows, it is recognized that there exist differences in demographic characteristics,

metabolic profile, and histological characteristics between lean and non-lean NAFLD patients. However, only a few studies investigated whether lean patients share similar, better, or worse prognoses compared to obese patients. Until now, data on this issue are still scanty and controversial. A Caucasian cohort included 1339 NAFLD patients determined by liver biopsy and followed up for 132 months (median 94 months). No significant

difference was observed in survival between lean and non-lean NAFLD patients (p = 0.069)10. Another study from Hong Kong had a similar result. The study enrolled 307 biopsy-confirmed NAFLD patients with a median follow-up of 49 months and no difference in the incidence of clinical events (a composite event of death,

cardiovascular and liver events, and malignancies) was observed between obese and non-obese NAFLD

patients (p = 0.190)18. A study from Sweden gives evidence that lean NAFLD patients had a better prognosis than obese NAFLD patients. This study included 646 biopsy-proven NAFLD patients with a median follow-up of

19.9 years. Compared to healthy controls, lean NAFLD patients had similar mortality (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.76– 1.41), while the obese NAFLD patients had a significantly higher risk of overall mortality (HR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.56– 2.74). Apart from these studies, an abstract reported the conclusion similar to our results that lean NAFLD

patients had the worse outcome in comparison with non-lean NAFLD patients11. With this gap, the study mainly

aimed to clarify the difference in long-term outcomes among NAFLD subgroups.

The result of the present study supports the conclusion that lean NAFLD had a higher all-cause mortality risk in comparison to overweight and obese NAFLD patients. The reason for the difference in long-term outcomes remains unclear, but potential explanations might be as follows: (1) Genome-wide association studies have demonstrated that steatosis-related single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), including TM6SF2, APOC3 rs2854116, and rs2854117 and genotype of the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing 3 (PNPLA3) C/G

or G/G are more prevalent in lean NAFLD patients19,20. Liver biopsy also suggests that lean NAFLD patients present worse histological steatosis, inflammation, a higher prevalence of steatohepatitis, and advanced

fibrosis compared to non-lean patients21,22. Worse histological features and higher risk of liver disease progression could lead to higher liver-related mortality in lean patients; (2) The accuracy and specificity of BMI in reflecting obesity and visceral adiposity are increasingly debated. BMI itself might fail to identify body fatness

in more than half of adults, and obesity may be greatly underestimated23. In addition, people with normal BMI

can have variable degrees of visceral adiposity, which predisposes to the development of fatty liver disease24,25; (3) Insulin resistance, obesity, and metabolic syndrome were closely associated with the incidence of NAFLD in

general26,27. In the present study, lean NAFLD patients presented with lower BMI, HOMA-IR, and better metabolic profiles. Whereas smoking was identified as an independent risk factor only in the lean NAFLD group. We hypothesize that together genetic predisposition, behavior, and environmental factors may play more

important roles in the poor prognosis of lean NAFLD; (4) Obesity constitutes a key determinant of awareness of NAFLD. Lean patients who are relatively normal in appearance are generally asymptomatic and their liver disease remains undiagnosed or delayed diagnosis, which could result in insufficient intervention and a worse prognosis. Unfortunately, we are unable to evaluate genetic or environmental parameters and liver-related mortality in this study. Further research is necessary to ascertain these hypotheses of lean NAFLD listed above.

The present study also added notable information on the metabolic profiles of lean NAFLD patients. It is well-

established that increased Lp(a) concentration is a strong cardiovascular risk factor28–30, while previous

studies demonstrated that Lp(a) was inversely associated with the presence of NAFLD31–33. A study reported

that high insulin concentrations suppressed apo(a) synthesis in hepatocytes34, and it was hypothesized that IR

may act as a mediator in the relationship between Lp(a) and NAFLD33. Results from the present study showed that Lp(a) concentrations were higher in lean NAFLD group with lower HOMA-IR, which was in accordance with

existing evidence. The prevalence of metabolic comorbidities including diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia was also lower in the lean NAFLD group compared with its overweight and obese counterparts. This information implies that the pathogenesis of patients with lean NAFLD differs from overweight or obese NAFLD patients and a more comprehensive and granular assessment of metabolic phenotypes beyond BMIbased approaches to NAFLD patients was needed.

Several limitations of this study should also be considered. First, we are unable to dynamic evaluate longitudinal changes in BMI and NAFLD status of participants since the NHANES III dataset does not conduct follow-up examinations. Second, we used the hepatic ultrasound result as the diagnosis standard of steatosis. However, it is neither practical nor feasible to perform liver biopsies on a vast population for its well-known limitations. Hepatic ultrasound could be regarded as a satisfactory assessment tool in the setting of a large population-

based epidemiologic study, and the accuracy of the assessment of NAHNES III was validated. Finally, although the all-cause mortality was confirmed higher in lean NAFLD patients, the risk of cardiovascular and cancer mortality among NAFLD subgroups was similar. We were unable to further ascertain whether the elevated allcause death risk was caused by higher liver-related mortality data since the NCHS restricts this information for public usage. Access to these restricted data could provide valuable knowledge in the context of lean NAFLD and liver-related deaths. Nevertheless, we believe that these limitations can be offset by the benefits of a large population-based study with the use of a nationally representative sample, the long duration of the follow-up

period, and the generalizability of our results to an ethnically diverse Western population in the US.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, in this national-wide cohort study, although patients with lean NAFLD had a better metabolic profile at baseline, an increased risk for long-term all-cause mortality during follow-up compared to patients with a higher BMI was found after adjustment of potential confounders. It is important to further characterize this population through well-designed studies, and our findings raise demands for a more comprehensive and granular assessment of metabolic phenotypes beyond BMI-based approaches to NAFLD patients.
